item.title: Russian FSB Router Targeting, Evilginx Microsoft 365 Phishing, and Claude Mythos Vulnerability Research
item.content:encoded:
US and allies warn of Russian critical infrastructure attacks — Must Read

Cybersecurity agencies from the U.S. and allied countries warn that Russian FSB-linked hackers are targeting critical infrastructure by abusing weakly configured routers, especially those using default SNMP settings and Cisco Smart Install flaws. Organizations are urged to harden network devices by upgrading to SNMPv3, disabling Smart Install, blocking risky traffic, patching firmware, and replacing end-of-life equipment.

  • Cybersecurity agencies from the United States and eight other countries issued a joint warning that Russian state hackers are targeting vulnerable and poorly configured routers to infiltrate critical infrastructure networks.
  • The joint advisory attributes the attacks to hackers from the Russian Federal Security Service Center 16, a group also tracked as Berserk Bear, Energetic Bear, Crouching Yeti, Dragonfly, Ghost Blizzard, and Static Tundra.
  • The group scans internet-connected IP address ranges for routers using default or common SNMP authentication strings, then copies device configuration files and exfiltrates them via TFTP to actor-controlled servers.
  • The sectors most at risk include energy, communications, defense industrial base, healthcare, financial services, defense, and state and local government services.
  • The advisory urges defenders to upgrade to SNMPv3, disable Cisco Smart Install, enforce strong unique passwords, block TFTP and SNMP traffic at edge firewalls, update software and firmware, and replace end-of-life devices.

Misconfigured Server Reveals Three Evilginx Phishing Operations Targeting Microsoft 365 — Should Read

A misconfigured phishing server exposed three Microsoft 365 phishing operations using Evilginx-based kits and device-code phishing to steal and refresh session tokens, showing how low the barrier has become for MFA-resistant account compromise. Defenders should pair phishing-resistant MFA with Conditional Access policies that block or tightly restrict Microsoft device code flow.

  • Lexfo found a publicly exposed Python web server with directory listing enabled that revealed phishing configurations, credential-harvesting logs, remote management installers, combolists, backup archives, and the operator’s Telegram session files.
  • The exposed server led researchers to three Microsoft 365 phishing operations, each using a custom fork of the open-source Evilginx proxy cloned from public GitHub repositories.
  • One operation attributed by Lexfo to the Egyptian actor codemado used an Evilginx adversary-in-the-middle proxy, SimpleHelp remote console access, the picis.net domain, and a bulk mailer called MaDoO Blaster.
  • The red-queen Evilginx fork from the Nigerian operator mail-argenta modified HTML attributes and URL rewriting behavior to evade checks and detection, and set a one-year lifetime on captured Microsoft session cookies.
  • The black-queen fork by saroula01 used Microsoft’s legitimate OAuth device code flow, where victims entered a real device code at microsoft.com/devicelogin and completed MFA on Microsoft’s own page while the attacker’s backend collected the resulting token.

When Mythos Owns The Loop: Self-Verifying Vulnerability Research — Should Read

Netskope used Anthropic’s Claude Mythos in self-verifying vulnerability research workflows against its own products, where separate model instances had to reproduce crashes or validate fixes before findings counted. The key takeaway is that frontier AI can now independently drive much of the vulnerability research loop, producing reproducible kernel, open-source, and binary-diff findings when grounded in strong verification harnesses.

  • Netskope used Anthropic’s Claude Mythos preview to run self-verifying vulnerability research against software that Netskope builds and ships.
  • Across three tracks, the model produced 9 kernel memory corruption findings behind a strict reachability bar, 17 previously unreported bugs in open source code used by Netskope products, and four confirmed n-day fixes reconstructed from a binary diff.
  • For kernel driver testing, a finding only counted when the model satisfied every runtime precondition between the entry point and unsafe sink and reproduced the crash three times from a clean snapshot.
  • For open source testing, findings had to be confirmed by a separate copy of Mythos in a clean sandbox against current upstream code using AddressSanitizer crashes.
  • For binary-diff testing, a patch-diff finding counted only if the same reproducer crashed the older build and ran cleanly on the latest build.
